extracted.intended_audience: general readers, media researchers, and television viewers interested in the history and practices of a US TV news magazine
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive documentation of the format, production practices, editorial norms, distribution, and controversies of the CBS news magazine '60 Minutes'. Useful for understanding how the program is produced, presented, and critiqued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magazine-format structure (three long-form stories)
rubrics_metrics.description: 60 Minutes normally has three long-form news stories without superimposed graphics. There is a commercial break between two stories. Each story is introduced from a set with a backdrop resembling pages from a magazine story on the same topic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The program undertakes its own investigations and follows up on investigations instigated by national newspapers and other sources. The magazine motif is explicit in staging and studio presentation (magazine-cover chroma keys, 'Vol. xx, No. xx' historically).

rubrics_metrics.name: On-camera presentation rule (journalists never share screen)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike its competitor 20/20, as well as traditional local and national news programs, the 60 Minutes journalists never share the screen with (or speak to) other 60 Minutes journalists on camera at any time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice 'creates a strong psychological sense of intimacy between the journalist and television viewers.' It is a formal stylistic rule of the program's on-air presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting tone and approach (reporter-centered investigation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The program was created to use a unique style of reporter-centered investigation, blending the journalism of See It Now and Edward R. Murrow; in Hewitt's words, 60 Minutes blends 'higher Murrow' and 'lower Murrow'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories aim to be of national importance but focus upon individuals involved with, or in conflict with, those issues. The program mixes in-depth investigative work and personality profiles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigative techniques pioneered (re-editing, hidden cameras, 'gotcha' visits)
rubrics_metrics.description: 60 Minutes pioneered many investigative journalism procedures and techniques, including re-editing interviews, hidden cameras, and 'gotcha journalism' visits to the home or office of an investigative subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These techniques are part of the program's historic toolkit but are presented historically and with acknowledgement of controversy and ethical debate (see controversies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Branding and pacing (stopwatch, opening sequence, correspondent intros)
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the show's inception the opening features a stopwatch. The opening sequence features a 'magazine cover' with the show's trademark Aristo stopwatch, intercut with preview clips; the sequence ends with each correspondent introducing themselves and a closing line 'Those stories tonight on 60 Minutes'. The stopwatch counts off each of the broadcast's 60 minutes and appears before each commercial break.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stopwatch design, background color, and intertitle have evolved (Aristo design, color changes in 2006, orientation changes). The stopwatch is used as an on-air pacing and branding device and is expected to 'display (within reasonable accuracy) the elapsed time of the episode to that point.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Scheduling and runtime norms
rubrics_metrics.description: The program generally airs Sundays at 7:00 p.m. Eastern (often delayed to 7:30 p.m. Eastern when CBS is airing late NFL games). The running time is 60 minutes including commercials; since the 2023–2024 season the show began to have occasional 90-minute episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically it moved into the Sunday evening slot permanently in December 1975. Start times vary regionally to accommodate sports and local programming; Pacific Time often starts at scheduled time because of earlier sports conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Segment length and recurring commentary pieces
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically the producers limited reports' airtime to around 13 minutes to maintain a magazine pacing. From 1978 to 2011 the program usually ended with Andy Rooney's light-hearted commentary pieces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mix of tightly timed investigative pieces and a concluding personality commentary became a recognizable structural pattern (and audience draw) for the program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Debate and point/counterpoint segments
rubrics_metrics.description: For most of the 1970s the program included Point/Counterpoint, in which a liberal and conservative commentator debated an issue (e.g., James J. Kilpatrick and Nicholas von Hoffman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The segment functioned as live competing editorials and became a notable innovation; revived formats (e.g., Clinton/Dole in 2003) were judged on tone and spiritedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplatform distribution and extra-content practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Videos and transcripts of 60 Minutes editions, as well as clips not included in the broadcast, are available on the program's website. Audio versions (without advertising) began to be distributed via podcast and iTunes Store starting September 23, 2007. Video (including full episodes) is made available for streaming several hours after broadcast on CBSNews.com and Paramount+. The program launched '60 Minutes Overtime' for further discussion and extra content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The program is also simulcast on several radio stations. Partnerships for extra content (historly with Yahoo!, etc.) have been used for distribution and audience engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification, authentication, and correction standards (fact-checking imperative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Controversies documented on the page show that failures to authenticate documents, insufficient corroboration of sources, misidentification of images, or missed red flags have led to corrections, on-air apologies, retractions, and personnel leaves (examples: Killian documents controversy, 'The Internet Is Infected' photo misidentification, Benghazi report retraction and correction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article implies expectations that the program authenticate key documents and forensic evidence, corroborate witness accounts with independent sources, consult experts, avoid presenting a single unchallenged perspective on contentious issues, and issue public corrections and conduct internal journalistic reviews when significant errors occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial independence and conflict-of-interest avoidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Incidents (notably Brown & Williamson reporting and decisions influenced by CBS legal and corporate concerns) illustrate the importance of editorial independence and avoiding conflicts of interest that could dilute reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The historical example shows that legal, corporate, or ownership pressures can lead to altered content or withheld evidence; maintaining independence from such pressures is presented implicitly as a standard for rigorous investigative journalism.
